brief.desc: Bearish, 42 of 100. Friday's 2.1 percent GLD gain was a thin half-day reflex off Wednesday's 15-month low and came with the dollar up. Real yields are 13bp higher and breakevens 23bp lower over 20 sessions, and GLD sits 9.6 percent below its 50-day average, so the trend drivers have not turned; confidence is moderate because the November 25 reversal looks like capitulation.
brief.yr: GLD closed at 334.40 dollars on November 27, up 2.12 percent from November 25, trading a tight 331.26 to 334.41 range and closing on the high on 6.7 million shares. December gold futures settled at 3,668.50 dollars; their 3.75 percent gain overstates the move because Wednesday's settle printed before GLD's late rally. DXY rose 0.33 percent to 104.01, so the dollar did not drive the move. This was a positioning bounce extending Wednesday's reversal from a 313.96 dollar intraday low.
brief.to: The base case (45 percent) is that the downtrend resumes toward about 315 dollars in GLD if jobs data are firm and real yields climb back above 2.90 percent; a 320 to 345 range is 35 percent and a squeeze toward 355 dollars is 20 percent. The key events are ISM Manufacturing on December 1, ISM Services on December 3 and November payrolls on December 4, plus delayed CFTC positioning data. This view flips bullish if the 10-year TIPS real yield (FRED DFII10) prints below 2.60 percent.
kf: Falling 10-year breakevens (2.12 percent, down 23bp in 20 sessions)
10-year TIPS real yield at 2.79 percent, up 13bp in 20 sessions
Speculative liquidation and technical damage (GLD 9.6 percent below its 50-day)

brief.why: The Fed-easing story should be bullish: the 2-year is down 25bp from its 4.88 percent November 13 high. It has not helped gold, because the bond market is reading the drop as disinflation, not accommodation. Breakevens slid from 2.35 to 2.12 percent in a month, so every basis point of nominal relief has gone into lower inflation compensation rather than lower real rates. DFII10 is still 2.79 percent; holding gold over TIPS costs nearly 280bp a year in real terms, and the inflation-hedge bid that justified this year's run is draining away. Then came the mechanical part. From November 16 to 25 real yields actually eased 13bp, yet GLD fell from 352.93 to a 313.96 intraday low. That decoupling looks like forced selling: specs cut Legacy Non-Commercial longs by 16,183 contracts in the week to November 17 alone, and the worst of the slide came after that snapshot. When gold falls while its main macro input is improving, the seller is the position, not the macro. The official sector is the floor, not the engine. Central banks added 321 tonnes in Q3, and 675 tonnes year-to-date is 6 percent ahead of last year (WGC). That demand is price-insensitive and slow: it absorbs liquidation but cannot reverse a trend set by real rates and spec exits, as the 34 percent drawdown from January shows. Friday's bounce fits the pattern of shorts and dip-buyers on a thin day after a capitulation-style reversal. A bounce is not a regime change until real yields roll over or breakevens stop falling.
brief.cons: The headlines have flipped to rebound, with FXStreet writing that bulls target 3,700 and that gold rebounds from a 15-month low (both November 27). Some outlets frame the Fed as leaning toward hikes (FinScans, November 27), which does not square with a 2-year down 25bp; FRED gets more weight than the headline. The crowded trade is now on the bearish side. Spec length was cut by 24k net contracts in one week, before the November 20 to 25 flush, so the short-term downside fuel is plausibly much thinner than the CFTC data shows. That is the strongest argument against pressing the bearish call: the easy money on the short has been made, and a Wednesday-style reversal on 17 million shares often marks a tradable low. The bounce narrative is right for a week; the new-leg-higher narrative needs a driver it does not yet have.
fals: Soften: GLD holds above 327.45 dollars (the November 25 close) through the December 4 payrolls, confirming a base; the call moves to neutral-leaning-bearish.
Invert: FRED DFII10 prints below 2.60 percent (the October 30 low), visible about one business day after each session; the call turns bullish.

Weak joint: the thesis assumes spec liquidation is unfinished, but the latest reconciled CFTC data is Legacy as of November 17, before the November 20 to 25 flush; if the next releases show managed money near flat, the bear case is overstated.
